one_liner: Educational benchmark of float-array sum kernels (unrolled, SIMD, threaded, GPU) against serial std::accumulate on a 1 GB array.
what_it_does: A Google Benchmark executable (plus a Rust criterion bench) that sums 268M floats with dozens of backends: an 8-accumulator unrolled loop, hand-written SSE/AVX2/AVX-512/NEON/SVE kernels, OpenMP, std::thread, fork_union, Taskflow, oneTBB arenas, std::reduce with par/par_unseq, and CUDA (CUB, Thrust, warp kernels). Each kernel is a small functor class in reduce_cpu.hpp constructed from (float const* begin, float const* end) and returning the sum; there is no library API, package or license.
how_it_is_fast: The single-thread gain over std::accumulate comes from breaking the serial floating-point add chain: std::accumulate must fold left to right, so each add waits for the previous one, while unrolled_gt keeps 8 independent accumulators that GCC can also vectorize. The hand-written kernels add SIMD lanes (one accumulator per kernel for SSE/AVX2/NEON/SVE, 2-16 ZMM accumulators with bidirectional traversal and non-temporal loads for AVX-512). Multicore variants split the array into cache-line-rounded per-core chunks with over-aligned partial sums, on huge pages and NUMA-bound memory.
when_to_use: Learning or teaching why a reassociating multi-accumulator loop beats std::accumulate by 2.6-7x on a memory-bound float sum (GCC 12, -O2 -march=native).
Measuring the memory-bandwidth ceiling of a many-core box: the multithreaded rows reach 368-550 GB/s on Zen4 and Graviton4 with std::reduce<par> or fork_union.
Comparing thread-pool dispatch latency on tiny inputs (PARALLEL_REDUCTIONS_LENGTH=1536): fork_union, Taskflow, OpenMP and std::thread, plus Rayon/Tokio/smol on the Rust side.
Starting point for your own reduction when you need f64 or Kahan accumulation over more than 2^24 elements, and will write your own tests on non-uniform data.
when_not_to_use: As a dependency: there is no LICENSE file (raw LICENSE 404, none in the sidebar), no API and no package, so the code cannot legally be copied.

Copying avx2_f64_t, avx512_f32unrolled_t or avx512_f32interleaving_t: all three return wrong sums on non-uniform input (see gotchas); the harness only ever feeds 1.0f, so the bugs never show in its error column.
Summing more than 2^24 values into a float accumulator: every f32 row in the README is wrong by 50-94% because each lane saturates at 16,777,216.
Expecting hand-written intrinsics to beat the compiler: on Zen4 and Graviton4 the plain unrolled loop is faster than the single-accumulator AVX2, NEON and SVE kernels.
As a source of AVX-512 numbers: the Zen4 1 GB AVX-512 rows were measured on kernels that read only half the array.

integration.dependencies: Google Benchmark v1.9.1, fmt 11.1.2, Taskflow v3.10.0, fork_union (main), all fetched by CMake; oneTBB (master) by default on Linux without CUDA; optional libnuma, BLAS, CUDA Toolkit with CCCL, OpenCL. Rust bench: rayon, tokio, async-executor, fork_union 0.3.3, criterion 0.6
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17), CMake; README results use GCC 12 and NVCC 12.1; code uses std::hardware_destructive_interference_size unconditionally
integration.platforms: Linux primary (mmap huge pages, libnuma); macOS via Homebrew LLVM; x86-64 SSE/AVX2/AVX-512 kernels and aarch64 NEON/SVE kernels, compiled in only when -march=native is set (GCC and NVCC paths only); CUDA GPUs
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; serial kernels are const functors over a const range, multithreaded wrappers own their pool and per-thread partial-sum slots and are not meant to be shared
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — kernels are functor classes over float const* ranges that only sum float input; not a std::accumulate replacement, and unlicensed

gotchas: The harness fills the array with 1.0f and checks only against n, which hides three reduction bugs in current main (confirmed by a self-written transcription test on patterned data): avx2_f64_t's double _mm256_hadd_pd returns 2*(lane0+lane1) and drops the upper 128-bit lane (1 instead of 16384 when only lane 3 is set); avx512_f32unrolled_t's combine adds fwd5/rev5 twice and drops fwd6/rev6 (20480 vs 16384); avx512_f32interleaving_t loads acc3 from it_begin+32 instead of +16 and acc4 from the same address as acc2, so it never reads every other 64-byte line, then drops acc4 and counts acc2 twice (0 vs 16384).

The Zen4 1 GB table predates commit a301c39 (2025-01-24, 'Fix: Measuring AVX-512 throughput'): at 9a5a61a the AVX-512 kernels advanced 32 floats per 16-float ZMM load, so they read half the array while bytes/s credited all of it. The 50% error on every avx512 row is that skip, not f32 saturation, so avx512<f32streamed> 19.27, <f32unrolled> 22.28 and <f32interleaving> 26.84 GB/s are invalid. Only the small-array latency-hiding table was re-run after the fix.

The f32 rows' error column comes from accumulator saturation at 2^24: std::accumulate<f32> 93.75%, unrolled/avx2 f32 50%, NEON/SVE 75%. Only f64, Kahan and std::reduce rows are exact, and the f64 SIMD rows are exact only because every lane holds the same value.

The AVX-512 kernels use aligned and non-temporal loads at both ends (it_end - 16*k), so both ends must be 64-byte aligned: lengths that are not a multiple of 16 floats can fault. USE_INTEL_TBB is defined as 0 or 1, so '#if defined(USE_INTEL_TBB)' always pulls in the oneTBB headers. Clang builds get no -march=native, so the AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels compile out.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over marcelcases/simd or Vectis when you care about a memory-bound 1 GB reduction across many backends (threads, std::reduce, CUDA/CUB) rather than an L1-resident single-core kernel. Vectis's scalar-4acc and -ffast-math rows are the better single-thread control, and EVE or VCL are the libraries to actually ship SIMD reductions with.
verified_claims_summary: With GCC 12 at effective -O2 -march=native, one thread summing 1 GB of 1.0f: the plain 8-accumulator unrolled loop reaches 14.74 (f64) and 28.23 (f32) GB/s on Graviton4 and 34.02/35.15 GB/s on Zen4 m7a, against serial std::accumulate's 5.58 and 4.88 GB/s (about 2.6-7.2x, derived from page data; only f64 is exact). The single-accumulator AVX2/NEON/SVE kernels land between the two, and multithreaded libstdc++ std::reduce<par> on oneTBB (368-550 GB/s) is the fastest CPU row.
status_note: Stale since 2025-07-22 (119 stars, not archived) and unlicensed, so it is reference only. The multi-accumulator f64 loop is sound teaching material, but avx2_f64_t, avx512_f32unrolled_t and avx512_f32interleaving_t give wrong sums on non-uniform data, and the Zen4 AVX-512 1 GB rows come from pre-fix kernels that read half the array.
